# Wills, powers of attorney and beneficiaries

What the estate planning lawyer covered at our meeting.

## What a will does

A will directs how the property in your own name is divided, names a personal representative, and names guardians for minor children. It controls only assets that go through probate. A will has no effect on accounts that pass by a form or by joint ownership.

## Who gets what: the form comes first

Retirement accounts such as an IRA or 401(k), life insurance and payable-on-death bank accounts go to the person named on the beneficiary designation form, whatever the will says. If the form names an ex-spouse and was never updated, the ex-spouse may receive the money. Check these forms after every marriage, divorce, birth or death. If no beneficiary is named, the money usually goes to the estate.

## Power of attorney

A durable power of attorney lets someone you choose handle money and property if you cannot. It ends at death; after that the personal representative named in the will takes over.

## Health care proxy

A health care proxy names who can make medical decisions when you cannot, and a living will states your wishes about life support. Give copies to your doctor and the person named.

## Where to keep the documents

Keep originals in a fireproof box at home or with the lawyer, tell the personal representative where they are, and do not put the only copy of a will in a safe-deposit box nobody else can open.

## Updating after life events

Review the will, the proxies and every beneficiary form every few years and after any big change: marriage, divorce, a child, a death, a move to another state.
